brief.situation: 08:00 med pass in a long-term care home. You are the LPN. Room 12A: Mr. Robert Hall, 84, heart failure and atrial fibrillation. His roommate in 12B is Mr. Robert Hale. The pharmacy delivered a new blister card of digoxin overnight.
handover: Night shift: Mr. Hall said he felt 'a bit queasy' at 06:00 and didn't want much breakfast.

MAR for Mr. Hall at 08:00: digoxin 0.125 mg (hold for an apical pulse below 60), metoprolol tartrate 25 mg (hold for HR below 60 or systolic below 100), furosemide 40 mg, potassium chloride 20 mEq. Potassium yesterday 4.1.
Both men are hard of hearing and both answer to 'Robert'.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check and each medication is its own step. You can give, hold, or set a medication aside.
Partway through you are asked to write what you found and what you will do. The case ends at 08:45, then a debrief scores what you did.

parts.label: Findings
parts.criteria: Names the wrong-strength digoxin card (0.25 mg dispensed, 0.125 mg ordered), the apical pulse below 60, the BP below metoprolol's parameter, and nausea, poor appetite and visual changes as possible digoxin toxicity; confirms the resident with two identifiers, not the room or the first name.
parts.modelAnswer: The digoxin card is 0.25 mg against an order for 0.125 mg. His apical pulse is 56 and his BP 96/58, both below the hold parameters, and he has nausea, poor appetite and yellow-tinged vision, which can be digoxin toxicity. I confirmed it is Mr. Hall with his band and date of birth, not by calling 'Robert'.

parts.label: What to do
parts.criteria: Holds digoxin and metoprolol and reports to the RN (and provider) with the data; gives furosemide and potassium as ordered; sets the card aside and tells the pharmacy; files an incident report for the near miss in the reporting system rather than the chart; documents the held doses and why.
parts.modelAnswer: Hold digoxin and metoprolol and report to the RN now with the pulse, BP and symptoms; give the furosemide and potassium. Set the wrong card aside and call the pharmacy. File an incident report in the reporting system for the near miss, not in his chart, and document the held doses with reasons.

expertPath.text: Compare each card with the MAR: digoxin card 0.25 mg, order 0.125 mg. Set it aside.
Two identifiers at 12A, not 'Robert?' at the door. Allergies and labs.
Apical pulse for a full minute (56), BP (96/58), ask about nausea and vision (yellow-tinged).
Hold digoxin and metoprolol; give furosemide and potassium. SBAR to the RN; call the pharmacy; incident report in the system; document the held doses and why.

bradycardia.headline: Symptomatic bradycardia
bradycardia.body: The rights include the right assessment before giving: an apical pulse for a full minute and the BP against the hold parameters. Find what you gave before you had them.

wrongResident.headline: Wrong resident
wrongResident.body: Room numbers and first names are not identifiers. Two identifiers, every time, at the bedside.

caught.headline: Caught in time
caught.body: The card checked against the MAR, two identifiers, data before giving, holds and reports, and the near miss in the reporting system. That is the expert path.

caughtGaps.headline: Safe, with gaps
caughtGaps.body: Nothing harmful reached him, but check the report to the RN, the pharmacy call and where the incident report went.

time_up.headline: A dose that should have been held
time_up.body: Find the check that would have stopped it.

scoring.modelReasoning: The rights are applied, not recited: compare each card with the MAR (the digoxin card is 0.25 mg against an order for 0.125 mg, so it is set aside and the pharmacy told); confirm the resident with two identifiers, never a room number or an answer to a first name; collect the data the orders require before giving (an apical pulse for a full minute before digoxin, the blood pressure and heart rate before metoprolol) and hold below the parameters; ask about nausea, appetite and visual changes as possible digoxin toxicity. Report the findings to the RN, give the medications that are safe, document held doses with the reason, and file an incident report for the near miss in the facility's reporting system, not the chart, so the system cause can be found.

incidentQ.ask: Where does the report of this near miss go?
incidentQ.explain: The incident reporting system. Near misses are reported so the system cause (here, a stock-bin error) can be fixed; the report is not part of the medical record, so the chart records only the care and the held doses.

fullMinute.ask: While you count: why a full minute at the apex rather than 15 seconds at the wrist?

choices.label: His rhythm is irregular, and digoxin decisions rest on the true rate
The two are always the same

fullMinute.explain: In atrial fibrillation some beats do not reach the wrist and a short count multiplies the error. Digoxin is held below 60, so the apical rate over a full minute is the number that decides.
